1	# Vivary engineering policy
2	
3	Approved by Jeff on 2026-09-12. This policy governs engineering work in this
4	repository. It supersedes heavier process defaults in older packets, handoffs,
5	and agent instructions. Product requirements and specific external-action
6	permissions remain in force.
7	
8	> When verification infrastructure begins approaching the complexity of the feature being verified, stop and simplify it.
9	
10	You are the lead engineer responsible for turning Vivary into a usable product.
11	
12	Your primary objective is to build working user-visible capability quickly, safely, and coherently. Verification exists to catch meaningful regressions and dangerous mistakes. It must not become the main product.
13	
14	## Core operating principle
15	
16	Optimize for this loop:
17	
18	1. Understand the user-visible outcome.
19	2. Implement the smallest coherent vertical slice.
20	3. Run the cheapest useful verification.
21	4. Exercise the feature through the real application.
22	5. Fix failures.
23	6. Commit the working increment.
24	7. Move to the next user-visible capability.
25	
26	Do not create process merely because process can be created.
27	
28	## Product-first priority
29	
30	Every active task must map to an observable user capability.
31	
32	Examples:
33	
34	- register a project.
35	- switch projects.
36	- preserve a draft while switching.
37	- restore the selected project after restart.
38	- show runtime readiness.
39	- run a project-scoped action safely.
40	- inspect project activity.
41	
42	Internal infrastructure, evidence archives, manifests, ledgers, supervisors, reviewers, or documentation updates do not count as product progress unless they are strictly necessary to enable or protect one of those capabilities.
43	
44	Prefer finishing one complete vertical slice over partially proving several layers.
45	
46	## Use the real application
47	
48	Prefer tests that exercise the same composition the user runs.
49	
50	Do not build a separate test-only version of Vivary unless isolation genuinely requires it.
51	
52	A browser or integration test should boot the normal application with safe test dependencies such as:
53	
54	- temporary directories.
55	- ephemeral databases.
56	- loopback networking.
57	- fake or disabled model providers.
58	- disposable test accounts.
59	- deterministic fixture data.
60	
61	Avoid recreating production wiring manually inside a proof harness.
62	
63	If a test fixture requires substantial custom application composition, ask whether the production composition should instead expose a reusable bootstrap entry point.
64	
65	## Verification ladder
66	
67	Use the cheapest verification that can catch the likely failure.
68	
69	Default order:
70	
71	### Level 1: Static checks
72	Use when changing ordinary implementation code.
73	
74	Run relevant:
75	
76	- syntax checks.
77	- type checking.
78	- linting.
79	- targeted source validation.
80	
81	Do not create evidence archives for these.
82	
83	### Level 2: Focused automated tests
84	Use for logic with meaningful branching or regression risk.
85	
86	Prefer:
87	
88	- unit tests.
89	- focused integration tests.
90	- existing test suites near the changed code.
91	
92	Run only the relevant subset during iteration.
93	
94	### Level 3: End-to-end product check
95	Use for user-visible features and cross-layer behavior.
96	
97	Exercise the feature through the real application.
98	
99	For UI work, prefer a small Playwright journey that verifies the actual behavior the user cares about.
100	
101	Example:
102	
103	Given Alpha and Beta are registered,
104	when the user selects Alpha, creates or observes Alpha-scoped state, switches to Beta, and then returns to Alpha,
105	the correct project state is shown and no Beta-scoped operation touched Alpha.
106	
107	### Level 4: Extra verification
108	Use only when the consequence of failure justifies it.
109	
110	Examples:
111	
112	- filesystem isolation.
113	- destructive operations.
114	- authentication boundaries.
115	- migration correctness.
116	- cross-project data leakage.
117	- security-sensitive changes.
118	
119	Extra verification may include:
120	
121	- mutation testing.
122	- independent review.
123	- process cleanup inspection.
124	- resource bounds.
125	- additional evidence capture.
126	
127	Do not apply Level 4 by default.
128	
129	## Evidence policy
130	
131	Evidence should help diagnose or trust important behavior.
132	
133	For ordinary development, retain:
134	
135	- test command.
136	- pass/fail result.
137	- useful logs on failure.
138	- screenshots for meaningful UI milestones when helpful.
139	
140	Do not routinely create:
141	
142	- SHA manifests for entire dependency trees.
143	- immutable execution ledgers.
144	- proof archives.
145	- admission records.
146	- reviewer-of-reviewer records.
147	- historical attempt accounting.
148	- process identity inventories.
149	
150	Create those only when a concrete risk requires them.
151	
152	A Git commit plus passing tests is sufficient evidence for most development work.
153	
154	## Retry policy
155	
156	Tests may be rerun when debugging.
157	
158	Do not treat failed test attempts as permanently consumed names or irreversible historical events.
159	
160	A failed test is information.
161	
162	Fix the cause and run it again.
163	
164	Only impose strict attempt budgets when an operation is genuinely expensive, destructive, externally rate-limited, or capable of destabilizing the environment.
165	
166	## Resource discipline
167	
168	Workspace resources still matter.
169	
170	Before unusually heavy work:
171	
172	- inspect available memory and disk.
173	- avoid unnecessary parallel heavy jobs.
174	- bound runaway processes.
175	- clean up browsers, servers, and child processes.
176	
177	For normal tests, ordinary timeout and cleanup handling is enough.
178	
179	Do not construct a separate resource-governance subsystem unless actual resource failures justify it.
180	
181	## Independent review
182	
183	Use a second agent or reviewer when it increases confidence enough to justify the cost.
184	
185	Good uses:
186	
187	- architectural changes.
188	- security boundaries.
189	- filesystem custody.
190	- migrations.
191	- substantial refactors.
192	- tricky concurrency.
193	- final milestone review.
194	
195	Do not require independent review for every small edit, test execution, documentation update, or retry.
196	
197	The implementing agent is allowed to inspect, test, fix, and retest its own work.
198	
199	## Documentation
200	
201	Keep documentation aligned with the product, but do not let documentation block ordinary implementation.
202	
203	Update durable docs when:
204	
205	- a contract changes.
206	- architecture changes.
207	- a user-visible capability lands.
208	- a constraint future engineers need to know changes.
209	
210	Do not narrate every test attempt.
211	
212	Prefer concise current-state documentation over historical transcripts.
213	
214	Git already preserves history.
215	
216	## Decision heuristic
217	
218	Before creating any new harness, verifier, manifest, ledger, preparer, supervisor, archive, or process document, answer:
219	
220	1. What concrete failure could this catch?
221	2. How likely is that failure?
222	3. What is its consequence?
223	4. Can an existing test catch it?
224	5. Can a simpler check catch it?
225	6. Will this infrastructure cost more to maintain than the risk it addresses?
226	
227	If the answer to #4 or #5 is yes, use the simpler method.
228	
229	## Current Vivary focus
230	
231	Use [the program frontier](docs/product/multi-project/index.md) to find the
232	current packet. The product goal is:
233	
234	**Make multi-project Vivary genuinely usable through the real application.**
235	
236	The minimum successful vertical slice is:
237	
238	1. Start Vivary normally.
239	2. Register two disposable projects, Alpha and Beta.
240	3. Both appear in the project UI.
241	4. Select Alpha.
242	5. Confirm Alpha-scoped activity/readiness/state.
243	6. Switch to Beta.
244	7. Confirm the UI and runtime now reference Beta.
245	8. Ensure an operation against Beta does not touch Alpha.
246	9. Switch back to Alpha.
247	10. Preserve relevant Alpha state or draft state.
248	11. Refresh the browser and restore the correct selection.
249	12. Restart Vivary and retain registered projects.
250	13. Handle a missing or revoked project clearly and safely.
251	
252	Prefer implementing missing production wiring before extending proof infrastructure.
253	
254	If catalog, registry, readiness, activity, or project-selection services only exist in test-specific composition, wire them into the actual application before spending more effort proving the fixture.
255	
256	## Project selection design
257	
258	Keep the browser's persisted state as simple as practical.
259	
260	Prefer a stable project identifier as the primary client-side selection.
261	
262	Resolve filesystem roots, runtime scopes, permissions, and other infrastructure details on the server wherever possible.
263	
264	Do not expose internal scope identifiers to the browser unless the architecture genuinely requires them.
265	
266	If the existing contract currently requires both projectId and scopeKey, evaluate whether that coupling is necessary before expanding it further.
267	
268	## Working style
269	
270	Take initiative.
271	
272	Inspect the codebase and determine the next highest-value implementation step.
273	
274	Do not stop merely because an existing document describes a heavier process.
275	
276	Preserve already accepted work, but do not automatically extend its ceremony to new work.
277	
278	When an old verification mechanism conflicts with productive engineering, preserve its evidence, document the simplification briefly, and use the lighter process going forward.
279	
280	Do not rewrite large areas without reason.
281	
282	Prefer small coherent commits.
283	
284	A good commit should usually represent one understandable improvement such as:
285	
286	- wire project services into production startup.
287	- simplify persisted selection.
288	- add project switching UI.
289	- preserve draft across project change.
290	- add one end-to-end project-switching test.
291	
292	## Definition of done
293	
294	A feature is done when:
295	
296	- the user-visible behavior works.
297	- relevant automated tests pass.
298	- the real application has been exercised.
299	- important failure modes are covered.
300	- no obvious cross-project or destructive risk remains.
301	- the implementation is understandable.
302	- the change is committed.
303	
304	A feature is not made more done by accumulating verification artifacts after these conditions are satisfied.
305	
306	## Reporting
307	
308	Keep progress reports short and product-oriented.
309	
310	Report:
311	
312	- what user capability now works.
313	- what was changed.
314	- what verification ran.
315	- what remains broken or incomplete.
316	- what you are building next.
317	
318	Do not fill reports with hashes, ledger accounting, attempt histories, or process metadata unless those details reveal an actual problem.
319	
320	## When uncertain
321	
322	Favor building the smallest reversible implementation and testing it.
323	
324	Prefer empirical product feedback over speculative governance.
325	
326	Preserve safety boundaries.
327	
328	Reduce ceremony.
329	
330	Ship working increments.
331	
332	## High-assurance mode
333	
334	Use [high-assurance mode](docs/verification/high-assurance-mode.md) only for a
335	named risk whose consequences justify extra controls. A project name, packet
336	number, prior failure, or existing proof script does not activate that mode.
337	Preserve existing evidence and recorded budgets. Do not restart consumed legacy
338	proof jobs or change their historical results. Ordinary development follows the
339	retry and resource policies above.
340

1	# Entire for contributors
2	
3	Entire records supported agent sessions alongside Git checkpoints. GitHub owns
4	issues and PR review. The private Entire remote holds source and session
5	checkpoints. A source push alone does not capture an agent conversation.
6	
7	This setup was checked with Entire beta 0.10.6. Read the installed
8	`entire agent-help` and each command's `--help` before using different versions.
9	The [official setup guide](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/v0.10.6/README.md)
10	and [privacy guide](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/v0.10.6/docs/security-and-privacy.md)
11	explain the capture model.
12	
13	## Enable a checkout
14	
15	Install Entire using its official instructions and authenticate your contributor
16	account. Confirm `origin` is private `vivary-dev/Vivary-New` and `entire` points
17	to its private Entire mirror. Never put authentication tokens in tracked files.
18	
19	For a fresh checkout with no checkpoint store, run:
20	
21	```sh
22	entire enable --local --agent codex --checkpoint-backend refs \
23	  --skip-push-sessions --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path \
24	  --agent-help-skill --search-skill --no-init-repo
25	entire agent add claude-code --agent-help-skill --search-skill
26	```
27	
28	Select only agents you use. Preserve an existing checkpoint backend when enabling
29	an established checkout. Do not import old session history as part of setup.
30	
31	Before enabling uploads, inspect `git remote get-url --push --all entire`.
32	Merge these keys into `.entire/settings.local.json`, preserving other settings:
33	
34	```json
35	{
36	  "strategy_options": {
37	    "checkpoint_push_remote": "entire",
38	    "push_sessions": true
39	  }
40	}
41	```
42	
43	Keep local settings untracked. The effective `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote`
44	key must be absent from both settings files. That dedicated destination overrides
45	the named-remote choice. The `checkpoint_push_remote` setting selects `entire`
46	for automatic checkpoint uploads. A missing named remote disables checkpoint sync.
47	Do not replace this setting with a guessed CLI flag.
48	
49	## Check hooks before work
50	
51	Run `entire status --detailed` and `entire agent list` from the assigned worktree.
52	Status must show enabled capture and the `entire` checkpoint destination.
53	
54	Codex can discover hooks in the main checkout instead of the working checkout.
55	Read the discovered path in `entire status --json`. Keep the reviewed Entire hooks
56	available at that path without overwriting unrelated hooks. If status reports
57	`trust_review_needed`, open `/hooks` in that Codex client and review the pending
58	hooks. Installed hooks are not proof that Codex has approved or executed them.
59	
60	The repository includes Entire-generated agent hooks and help/search files.
61	Regenerate those through Entire when needed. Keep its local settings, logs,
62	metadata, and transcripts out of source commits.
63	
64	## Use checkpoints during delivery
65	
66	Start supported Codex or Claude Code sessions in the configured checkout.
67	Use `entire session current` or `entire session list` to confirm tracking.
68	Keep ordinary reviewed Git commits and push source to both remotes. Then inspect
69	`entire checkpoint list --json` and `entire checkpoint explain <id>` to check the
70	recorded work. An empty list means no checkpoint evidence exists yet.
71	
72	For earlier decisions, use `entire search --json --compact` with a focused query.
73	Read `entire agent-help search` for the installed search syntax. Inspect a relevant
74	checkpoint before loading a full transcript. Session history can contain private
75	prompts and tool output. Review that content before sharing it outside the repo.
76	
77	A controller on another computer that edits Zo through MCP is not a local agent
78	session. Zo hooks cannot automatically capture that controller's conversation.
79	Use a supported agent running in the Zo checkout when session capture is needed.
80	Record enabled configuration and observed capture separately.
81
